claim: Classical genes within the Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) are responsible for peptide presentation to T cells.
source: Classical genes within the Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) are responsible for peptide presentation to T cells, thus playing a central role in immune defense against pathogens.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about MHC function.

claim: Classical MHC genes play a central role in immune defense against pathogens.
source: Classical genes within the Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) are responsible for peptide presentation to T cells, thus playing a central role in immune defense against pathogens.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about MHC function.

claim: MHC genes are subject to strong selective pressures including both balancing and directional selection.
source: These genes are subject to strong selective pressures including both balancing and directional selection, resulting in exceptional genetic diversity—thousands of alleles per gene in humans.
evidence: This is supported by citations throughout the paper and established knowledge in the field.

claim: MHC genes exhibit exceptional genetic diversity with thousands of alleles per gene in humans.
source: These genes are subject to strong selective pressures including both balancing and directional selection, resulting in exceptional genetic diversity—thousands of alleles per gene in humans.
evidence: This is supported by references to databases and literature (Maccari et al., 2017; Maccari et al., 2020; Robinson et al., 2019).

claim: Some MHC allelic lineages appear to be shared between primate species through trans-species polymorphism (TSP).
source: Moreover, some allelic lineages appear to be shared between primate species, a phenomenon known as trans-species polymorphism (TSP) or incomplete lineage sorting, which is rare in the genome overall.
evidence: This is a central claim of the paper supported by phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Trans-species polymorphism is rare in the genome overall.
source: Moreover, some allelic lineages appear to be shared between primate species, a phenomenon known as trans-species polymorphism (TSP) or incomplete lineage sorting, which is rare in the genome overall.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Leffler et al., 2013 in the paper.

claim: There is strong support for ancient TSP in 7 of 10 classical MHC genes.
source: We find strong support for ancient TSP in 7 of 10 classical genes, including—remarkably—between humans and old-world monkeys in MHC-DQB1.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by Bayes factor analysis shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: There is trans-species polymorphism between humans and old-world monkeys in MHC-DQB1.
source: We find strong support for ancient TSP in 7 of 10 classical genes, including—remarkably—between humans and old-world monkeys in MHC-DQB1.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic trees and Bayes factors shown in Figure 2B and Figure 4.

claim: Ancient MHC lineages have been maintained by balancing selection for at least 31 million years.
source: Together, these results suggest complex selective forces—arising from differential peptide binding—that drive short-term allelic turnover within lineages while also maintaining deeply divergent lineages for at least 31 million years in some cases.
evidence: This is inferred from the TSP between humans and OWM, whose divergence is dated to 31 MYA.

claim: The most rapidly-evolving amino acid positions in MHC genes are extremely enriched for autoimmune and infectious disease associations.
source: The most rapidly-evolving amino acid positions are extremely enriched for autoimmune and infectious disease associations.
evidence: This is supported by the literature search and analysis shown in Table 1 and Figure 6—figure supplement 7.

claim: The MHC is a large locus containing many immune genes shared among jawed vertebrates.
source: The Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) is a large locus containing many immune genes that is shared among the jawed vertebrates (Radwan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In humans, the MHC is also known as the HLA (Human Leukocyte Antigen) region.
source: In humans, the MHC is also known as the HLA (Human Leukocyte Antigen) region; it spans about 5 megabases (Mb) on chromosome 6 and contains 412 genes (Figure 1A; Genome Reference Consortium, 2022; O'Leary et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established nomenclature supported by citations.

claim: The human MHC/HLA region spans about 5 megabases on chromosome 6 and contains 412 genes.
source: In humans, the MHC is also known as the HLA (Human Leukocyte Antigen) region; it spans about 5 megabases (Mb) on chromosome 6 and contains 412 genes (Figure 1A; Genome Reference Consortium, 2022; O'Leary et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by database references and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: MHC peptide presentation allows T cells to monitor the body for the presence of foreign peptides.
source: MHC peptide presentation allows T cells to monitor the body for the presence of foreign peptides, which might indicate infection or cancer; this is crucial for vertebrate immune surveillance (Neefjes et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about MHC function supported by citation.

claim: MHC peptide presentation is crucial for vertebrate immune surveillance.
source: MHC peptide presentation allows T cells to monitor the body for the presence of foreign peptides, which might indicate infection or cancer; this is crucial for vertebrate immune surveillance (Neefjes et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Nucleotide diversity in the human MHC exceeds 70 times the genome-wide average near the classical genes.
source: Indeed, modern data show that nucleotide diversity in the human MHC (HLA region) exceeds 70 times the genome-wide average near the classical genes, suggesting ancient balancing selection (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is calculated from 1000 Genomes data and shown in Figure 1.

claim: High nucleotide diversity in the MHC suggests ancient balancing selection.
source: Indeed, modern data show that nucleotide diversity in the human MHC (HLA region) exceeds 70 times the genome-wide average near the classical genes, suggesting ancient balancing selection (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is inferred from the observed high diversity shown in Figure 1.

claim: Only approximately 100 loci genome-wide show compelling evidence for sharing of ancestral alleles between humans and chimpanzees.
source: Indeed, only ∼100 loci genome-wide show compelling evidence for sharing of ancestral alleles between humans and our closest relatives, chimpanzees (Leffler et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Leffler et al., 2013.

claim: Besides the MHC, the only other clear example of deep TSP in primates is at the ABO locus.
source: TSP among humans and more distantly related species is even rarer; besides the MHC, the only other clear example of deep TSP is at the ABO locus (which influences blood type; Azevedo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Azevedo et al., 2015.

claim: At the ABO locus, both the A and B alleles are shared by descent throughout the apes.
source: At this locus, both the A and B alleles are shared by descent throughout the apes, implying that the A and B lineages date back to at least the divergence point of humans and gibbons 23 MY ago (Ségurel et al., 2012; Kuderna et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ségurel et al., 2012 and Kuderna et al., 2023.

claim: The A and B lineages at the ABO locus date back to at least 23 million years ago.
source: At this locus, both the A and B alleles are shared by descent throughout the apes, implying that the A and B lineages date back to at least the divergence point of humans and gibbons 23 MY ago (Ségurel et al., 2012; Kuderna et al., 2023).
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution and supported by citations.

claim: MHC-C shows strong support for TSP within the African apes: human, chimpanzee, and gorilla.
source: At the Class I genes (Figure 3), MHC-C shows strong support for TSP within the African apes: human, chimpanzee, and gorilla.
evidence: This is supported by Bayes factors shown in Figure 3.

claim: MHC-C has maintained some allelic lineages for most of its history.
source: Having arisen fairly recently in the ancestor of human and orangutan, MHC-C has thus maintained some allelic lineages for most of its history.
evidence: This is inferred from the TSP analysis and the known age of the gene.

claim: TSP has not previously been reported for MHC-C.
source: TSP has not previously been reported for this gene.
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding of the study.

claim: MHC-A has had a long history of gene conversion affecting different exons.
source: Past work suggests that this gene has had a long history of gene conversion affecting different exons, resulting in different evolutionary histories for different parts of the gene (Hans et al., 2017; Gleimer et al., 2011; Adams and Parham, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The lack of concordance in Bayes factors across different exons for MHC-A is evidence for gene conversion rather than balancing selection.
source: As shown in Figure 3, the lack of concordance in Bayes factors across the different exons for MHC-A is evidence for gene conversion, rather than balancing selection, being the most important factor in this gene's evolution.
evidence: This is inferred from the Bayes factor analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The Bayes factors for MHC-E, -F, and -G show strong evidence against TSP.
source: The Bayes factors for all three of these genes show strong evidence against TSP, as expected.
evidence: This is supported by the Bayes factor analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: MHC-E has a known balanced polymorphism in humans with two main alleles at similar frequencies worldwide.
source: Interestingly, despite its non-classical role, MHC-E has a known balanced polymorphism in humans; the two main alleles are at similar frequencies worldwide but may have different expression levels and peptide preferences (Paganini et al., 2019; Grant et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Paganini et al., 2019 and Grant et al., 2020.

claim: The balanced polymorphism in MHC-E is young.
source: Our approach—meant to detect ancient TSP—does not reveal balancing selection in MHC-E, showing that this balanced polymorphism is young.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of TSP signal in the analysis.

claim: MHC-DPA1 shows TSP between human, chimpanzee, and gorilla in exon 2, but not in exon 3.
source: MHC-DPA1 shows TSP between human, chimpanzee, and gorilla in exon 2, but not in exon 3.
evidence: This is supported by Bayes factors shown in Figure 4.

claim: TSP in MHC-DPA1 is less deep than has been previously suggested with non-Bayesian methods.
source: We find that this TSP in MHC-DPA1 is less deep than has been previously suggested with non-Bayesian methods (Otting and Bontrop, 1995), underscoring the importance of this methodology for handling the MHC.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with previous work cited (Otting and Bontrop, 1995).

claim: MHC-DPB1 shows strong evidence for TSP between human and orangutan in exon 3.
source: Meanwhile, its partner MHC-DPB1 shows strong evidence for TSP between human and orangutan in exon 3 and suggestive evidence in exon 2; our work provides the first evidence of TSP between humans and other apes for this gene (Slierendregt et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by Bayes factors shown in Figure 4.

claim: This work provides the first evidence of TSP between humans and other apes for MHC-DPB1.
source: Meanwhile, its partner MHC-DPB1 shows strong evidence for TSP between human and orangutan in exon 3 and suggestive evidence in exon 2; our work provides the first evidence of TSP between humans and other apes for this gene (Slierendregt et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding with reference to previous work.

claim: The MHC-DRA gene is conserved across species with little polymorphism.
source: The MHC-DRA gene is conserved across species with little polymorphism, while the MHC-DRB region is highly variable both in gene content and allelic diversity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MHC-DR genes.

claim: The MHC-DRB region is highly variable both in gene content and allelic diversity.
source: The MHC-DRA gene is conserved across species with little polymorphism, while the MHC-DRB region is highly variable both in gene content and allelic diversity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MHC-DR genes.

claim: Bayes factors for the MHC-DRA gene reveal strong evidence against TSP for all species pairs.
source: Consistent with this, Bayes factors for the MHC-DRA gene reveal strong evidence against TSP for all species pairs, while MHC-DRB1 shows strong evidence in favor of TSP between human, chimpanzee, gorilla, OWM, and even NWM in exon 2.
evidence: This is supported by Bayes factors shown in Figure 4.

claim: MHC-DRB1 shows strong evidence in favor of TSP between human, chimpanzee, gorilla, OWM, and NWM in exon 2.
source: Consistent with this, Bayes factors for the MHC-DRA gene reveal strong evidence against TSP for all species pairs, while MHC-DRB1 shows strong evidence in favor of TSP between human, chimpanzee, gorilla, OWM, and even NWM in exon 2.
evidence: This is supported by Bayes factors shown in Figure 4.

claim: Only three MHC-DRB genes are truly orthologous between apes and OWM.
source: We show in our companion paper that individual MHC-DRB genes are short-lived, and only three are truly orthologous between apes and OWM (Fortier and Pritchard, 2025).
evidence: This is supported by analysis in the companion paper.

claim: The MHC-DQB1 gene shows definitive evidence for TSP back to at least the ancestor of humans and OWM.
source: Remarkably, the MHC-DQB1 gene shows definitive evidence for TSP back to at least the ancestor of humans and OWM.
evidence: This is supported by Bayes factors shown in Figure 4 and phylogenetic trees in Figure 2B.

claim: Allelic lineages at MHC-DQB1 have been maintained for over 31 million years.
source: While this result has been presented previously, we confirm it with decisive evidence (Bayes factor >100) for allelic lineages being maintained for over 31 MY (Otting et al., 1992; Otting et al., 2002; Loisel et al., 2006; Simons et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by Bayes factors and confirmed with citations to previous work.

claim: There is very strong evidence for TSP between all groups of OWM for MHC-DPA1, -DPB1, -DQA1, and -DQB1.
source: We see very strong evidence for TSP between all groups of OWM for MHC-DPA1, -DPB1, -DQA1, and -DQB1, indicating that allelic lineages at these genes have been maintained within the OWM for at least 19 MY.
evidence: This is supported by Bayes factors shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Allelic lineages at MHC-DPA1, -DPB1, -DQA1, and -DQB1 have been maintained within the OWM for at least 19 million years.
source: We see very strong evidence for TSP between all groups of OWM for MHC-DPA1, -DPB1, -DQA1, and -DQB1, indicating that allelic lineages at these genes have been maintained within the OWM for at least 19 MY.
evidence: This is inferred from the TSP analysis and known divergence times.

claim: MHC-E shows evidence for 15-million-year-old TSP within the OWM.
source: MHC-E, a gene that is non-classical in humans and is presumed non-classical in OWM (yet is duplicated in some species), shows evidence for 15-MY-old TSP within the OWM.
evidence: This is supported by Bayes factors shown in supplementary figures.

claim: In non-classical MHC-DMB, TSP within the OWM is as old as 11 million years.
source: In non-classical MHC-DMB, we also observe TSP within the OWM as old as 11 MY.
evidence: This is supported by Bayes factors shown in supplementary figures.

claim: TSP is more ancient among the Class II genes than the Class I genes.
source: Overall, TSP is more ancient among the Class II genes than the Class I genes, consistent with the genes' older age.
evidence: This is inferred from the Bayes factor results across gene classes.

claim: In classical genes MHC-B and -C, nearly all the rapidly-evolving sites lie within exons 2 and 3.
source: In classical genes MHC-B and -C, nearly all the rapidly-evolving sites lie within exons 2 and 3, which encode the protein's peptide-binding domain.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Exons 2 and 3 encode the peptide-binding domain in Class I MHC proteins.
source: In classical genes MHC-B and -C, nearly all the rapidly-evolving sites lie within exons 2 and 3, which encode the protein's peptide-binding domain.
evidence: This is established knowledge about MHC protein structure.

claim: In MHC-B, exons 2 and 3 contain 94% of the sites evolving at more than four times the baseline evolutionary rate.
source: While exons 2 and 3 make up only ∼50% of the gene's length, they contain 94% and 90% of the sites evolving at more than four times the baseline evolutionary rate for the classical genes MHC-B and MHC-C, respectively.
evidence: This is calculated from the BEAST2 evolutionary rate analysis.

claim: In MHC-C, exons 2 and 3 contain 90% of the sites evolving at more than four times the baseline evolutionary rate.
source: While exons 2 and 3 make up only ∼50% of the gene's length, they contain 94% and 90% of the sites evolving at more than four times the baseline evolutionary rate for the classical genes MHC-B and MHC-C, respectively.
evidence: This is calculated from the BEAST2 evolutionary rate analysis.

claim: In MHC-B, exons 2 and 3 each show significantly higher proportions of rapidly-evolving sites compared to the 'other' exons.
source: In MHC-B, exons 2 and 3 each show significantly higher proportions of rapidly-evolving sites compared to the 'other' exons (exons in the gene excluding 2, 3, or 4), while the difference is not significant for MHC-C (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown by statistical testing in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Non-classical MHC-E has fewer rapidly-evolving sites than the classical genes.
source: As shown in Figure 5A, this gene has fewer rapidly-evolving sites than the classical genes.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In MHC-E, rapidly-evolving sites are relatively evenly distributed across the gene.
source: These sites are also relatively evenly distributed across the gene, with exons 2 and 3 (which cover ∼50% of the gene's length) containing 45% of the sites evolving at over four times the baseline evolutionary rate.
evidence: This is calculated from the BEAST2 evolutionary rate analysis.

claim: MHC-E has been remarkably conserved across the primates.
source: These results support that MHC-E has been remarkably conserved across the primates and that its evolution may not be driven by differential peptide binding (Heijmans et al., 2020).
evidence: This is inferred from the evolutionary rate analysis and supported by citation.

claim: In MHC-B and -C, rapidly-evolving amino acids tend to be located within the peptide-binding groove.
source: In MHC-B and -C, rapidly-evolving amino acids (orange) tend to be located within the peptide-binding groove.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: For MHC-B, -C, and -E, amino acids closer to the peptide have significantly higher evolutionary rates than amino acids further from the peptide.
source: For all three proteins, amino acids closer to the peptide have significantly higher evolutionary rates than amino acids further from the peptide, as shown in Figure 5C (see also Figure 5—figure supplements 4 and 5).
evidence: This is shown by regression analysis in Figure 5C.

claim: Rapid evolution and diversity at the classical MHC genes is mediated by selective pressures for changes in peptide binding.
source: These results are consistent with the expectation that rapid evolution and diversity at the classical MHC genes would be mediated by selective pressures for changes in peptide binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between evolutionary rate and distance to peptide.

claim: Exon 2 makes up approximately 30% of the coding region in Class II MHC genes.
source: Exon 2, which makes up ∼30% of the coding region, contains 32% of sites evolving at more than twice the baseline rate in MHC-DRA, but 57% of such sites in MHC-DQA, 61% in MHC-DQB, and 73% in MHC-DRB.
evidence: This is calculated from the gene structure and evolutionary rate analysis.

claim: In MHC-DRB, exon 2 contains 73% of sites evolving at more than twice the baseline rate.
source: Exon 2, which makes up ∼30% of the coding region, contains 32% of sites evolving at more than twice the baseline rate in MHC-DRA, but 57% of such sites in MHC-DQA, 61% in MHC-DQB, and 73% in MHC-DRB.
evidence: This is calculated from the BEAST2 evolutionary rate analysis.

claim: Exon 2 contains a significantly higher proportion of rapidly-evolving sites compared to the 'other' exons in classical MHC-DQA, -DQB, -DRB, and -DPB.
source: Comparing across exons, exon 2 contains a significantly higher proportion of rapidly-evolving sites compared to the "other" exons in classical MHC-DQA, -DQB, -DRB, and -DPB, but also—curiously—in non-classical MHC-DMA and -DMB (Figure 6—figure supplements 2 and 4).
evidence: This is shown by statistical testing in Figure 6—figure supplements 2 and 4.

claim: Non-classical MHC-DMA and -DMB show significantly higher proportions of rapidly-evolving sites in exon 2.
source: Comparing across exons, exon 2 contains a significantly higher proportion of rapidly-evolving sites compared to the "other" exons in classical MHC-DQA, -DQB, -DRB, and -DPB, but also—curiously—in non-classical MHC-DMA and -DMB (Figure 6—figure supplements 2 and 4).
evidence: This is shown by statistical testing in Figure 6—figure supplements 2 and 4.

claim: MHC-DM shapes the repertoire of peptides presented by MHC-DR, favoring high-affinity peptides.
source: MHC-DM thus shapes the repertoire of peptides presented by MHC-DR, favoring high-affinity peptides (Dijkstra and Yamaguchi, 2019; Schulze and Wucherpfennig, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Host-pathogen evolution shaping the MHC-DRB genes may have resulted in co-evolution of MHC-DMA and -DMB.
source: It is plausible that the host-pathogen evolution shaping the MHC-DRB genes has resulted in co-evolution of MHC-DMA and -DMB to maintain this regulatory interaction.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observed rapid evolution in MHC-DMA and -DMB.

claim: For MHC-DQA, -DQB, and -DRB, amino acids closer to the peptide had significantly higher evolutionary rates.
source: For the other three proteins, amino acids closer to the peptide had significantly higher evolutionary rates.
evidence: This is shown by regression analysis in Figure 6C.

claim: MHC-DRA did not show a significant relationship between evolutionary rate and distance to peptide.
source: MHC-DRA did not show a significant relationship between evolutionary rate and distance, as expected by its relatively uniform distribution of evolutionary rates across the sequence (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is shown by regression analysis in Figure 6C.

claim: Differential peptide binding and TCR responsiveness drive the diversity and long-term balancing selection at the classical genes.
source: This is consistent with differential peptide binding and TCR responsiveness driving the diversity and long-term balancing selection at the classical genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between evolutionary rate and distance to peptide.

claim: The majority of rapidly-evolving positions in MHC-B have at least one disease or trait association.
source: The majority of rapidly-evolving positions in MHC-B have at least one association.
evidence: This is shown in Table 1.

claim: All three classical Class I genes (MHC-A, -B, and -C) show a significant positive relationship between per-amino-acid evolutionary rate and the number of amino acid associations.
source: Furthermore, all three classical Class I genes (MHC-A, -B, and -C) show a significant positive relationship between per-amino-acid evolutionary rate and the number of amino acid associations (Figure 6—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is shown by regression analysis in Figure 6—figure supplement 7.

claim: The relationship between evolutionary rate and number of associations is not significant for the Class II genes.
source: Interestingly, this relationship is not significant for the Class II genes, possibly because they evolve more slowly overall.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 7 and inferred from the analysis.

claim: MHC-DQB1 exhibits trans-species polymorphism spanning at least 31 million years, placing it among the most ancient examples of balancing selection known in any species.
source: Our evidence for TSP at MHC-DQB1 spanning at least 31 MY places it among the most ancient examples of balancing selection known in any species, and almost certainly the oldest in primates.
evidence: This is inferred from the TSP analysis and comparison with other known examples.

claim: The deepest example of TSP within primates aside from MHC is at the ABO locus with an age of 23 million years.
source: Aside from MHC, the deepest example within primates is at the ABO locus controlling blood type; it exhibits trans-species polymorphism between humans and gibbons, an age of 23 MY (Ségurel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ségurel et al., 2012.

claim: In various chimpanzee species, OAS1 contains alleles up to 13 million years old.
source: In various chimpanzee species, OAS1, which helps inhibit viral replication, contains alleles up to 13 MY old (Ferguson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ferguson et al., 2012.

claim: TSP between chimpanzee and human includes LAD1, a protein that maintains cell cohesion, with an age of 6 million years.
source: TSP between chimpanzee and human includes LAD1, a protein that maintains cell cohesion (6 MY; Teixeira et al., 2015), retroviral transcription factor TRIM5α (4-7 MY in apes and >8 MY in OWM; Cagliani et al., 2010; Newman et al., 2006), and ZC3HAV1, an antiviral protein leading to viral RNA degradation (6 MY; Cagliani et al., 2012), among others (Leffler et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Teixeira et al., 2015.

claim: MHC polymorphisms have been maintained for 35 million years in cetaceans.
source: Several of the oldest examples are found in the MHC locus: MHC polymorphisms have been maintained for 35 MY in cetaceans (Xu et al., 2009), 40 MY in herons (Li et al., 2011), 48 MY in mole rats (Kundu and Faulkes, 2007), 70 MY in tree frogs (Zhao et al., 2013), and over 105 MY in salmonid fishes (Kiryu et al., 2005; Grimholt et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2009.

claim: The most rapidly-evolving codons at MHC are substituted at around two- to fourfold the baseline rate.
source: Indeed, within the phylogeny, we find that the most rapidly-evolving codons are substituted at around two- to fourfold the baseline rate, generating ample mutations upon which selection may act.
evidence: This is calculated from the BEAST2 evolutionary rate analysis.

claim: For classical genes except MHC-DRA, rapidly-evolving sites lie within the peptide binding regions of the corresponding proteins.
source: For the classical genes (except MHC-DRA), these rapidly-evolving sites lie within the peptide binding regions of the corresponding proteins, usually very close to the peptide-contact surfaces.
evidence: This is shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Selection at the MHC is mainly driven by the peptide presentation pathway.
source: This does not hold true for the non-classical genes, supporting the fact that selection at the MHC is mainly driven by the peptide presentation pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the contrast between classical and non-classical genes.

claim: Rapidly-evolving amino acids in MHC are associated with shaping T cell receptor (TCR) repertoires.
source: The primary role of classical MHC proteins is to present peptides for T cell recognition; we found that the same rapidly-evolving amino acids are associated with shaping T cell receptor (TCR) repertoires.
evidence: This is shown in Table 1 and supported by literature associations.

claim: Rapidly-evolving amino acids in MHC are frequently associated with autoimmune and infectious diseases in HLA fine-mapping studies.
source: Moreover, these amino acids are frequently associated with autoimmune and infectious diseases in HLA fine-mapping studies, particularly for Class I.
evidence: This is shown in Table 1 and Figure 6—figure supplement 7.

claim: In response to rapidly-changing pathogen pressures, the peptide-binding regions of classical MHC proteins evolve to bind changing pathogen antigens.
source: In response to rapidly-changing pathogen pressures, the PBRs of classical MHC proteins evolve to bind changing pathogen antigens and present them to TCRs.
evidence: This is inferred from the evolutionary analysis and known MHC function.

claim: Broad lineages of MHC alleles are maintained over tens of millions of years by strong balancing selection.
source: Broad lineages of MHC alleles are maintained over tens of millions of years by strong balancing selection, providing defense against a wide variety of different pathogens.
evidence: This is inferred from the TSP analysis.

claim: Within MHC lineages, alleles turn over quickly in response to new specific threats.
source: Yet within these lineages, alleles turn over quickly in response to new specific threats.
evidence: This is inferred from the evidence of both ancient TSP and rapid evolution.

claim: As MHC proteins evolve, there is an unavoidable flux between infection defense and autoimmune susceptibility.
source: As MHC proteins evolve, there is an unavoidable flux between infection defense and autoimmune susceptibility.
evidence: This is inferred from the disease associations with rapidly-evolving sites.

claim: Rapidly-evolving amino acids in MHC are associated with both infections and autoimmune conditions.
source: As a result, rapidly-evolving amino acids are associated with both infections and autoimmune conditions.
evidence: This is shown in Table 1.

claim: The vast majority of nonhuman MHC sequences were obtained via Sanger sequencing or next-generation sequencing methods.
source: One limitation of the data we used is that the vast majority of nonhuman MHC sequences were obtained via Sanger sequencing or next-generation sequencing methods.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the data sources.

claim: PCR-related technical artifacts such as heteroduplexes and chimeras can affect MHC sequencing.
source: While highly accurate sequence-wise, these methods are limited by PCR-related technical artifacts such as heteroduplexes and chimeras.
evidence: This is established knowledge about sequencing limitations.

claim: Long-read sequencing of the MHC region has the potential to solve many sequencing and assembly issues.
source: Luckily, long-read sequencing of the MHC region has the potential to solve many of these issues.
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent work using long-read sequencing.

claim: Oxford Nanopore and PacBio HiFi sequencing have been used to obtain high-quality MHC sequences in humans.
source: Oxford Nanopore and PacBio HiFi sequencing have already been used to obtain high-quality MHC sequences in humans (Wenger et al., 2019; Jain et al., 2018; Liu, 2021; Bruijnesteijn, 2023), and researchers are beginning to explore their potential in non-model organisms (Cheng et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.
